passage: At fifteen, Urmila had two friends who praised her drawing. Deepak said it was perfect every single time, and then asked to copy her chemistry homework. Rukmini said, "The faces are lovely, but the hands look stiff. Try again?" Urmila bristled, then looked at the page and saw it. She noticed that Deepak's compliments always arrived just before a favour, and that Rukmini asked for nothing at all. It was Rukmini's kind of honesty that she began to trust. At twenty-five, Urmila ran a small design studio. A supplier, Deepak's cousin, told her at the door, "You have the best eye in the city. Sign off on this order today and I'll give you the early rate." She smiled and thanked him warmly. "That's kind. I'll look at the numbers tonight and tell you tomorrow." She did not sign. At home she compared the quote with two others and found it was higher. The next morning she called him, polite and clear, to decline. She still remembered the kind words fondly, because they were kind, but they had not decided anything.

qa.q: What did Rukmini say about Urmila's drawing?
qa.a: She said the faces were lovely but the hands looked stiff.

qa.q: How does Urmila's view of Deepak and Rukmini at fifteen relate to how she treats the supplier at twenty-five?
qa.a: At fifteen she saw that Deepak's compliments came before a favour, while Rukmini praised and disagreed and asked for nothing. At twenty-five she thanked the supplier warmly but waited and compared quotes, so praise did not decide the order.

qa.q: What was Urmila probably feeling when Rukmini said the hands looked stiff?
qa.a: She felt stung and defensive at first, then honest recognition when she saw it herself.

qa.q: What could Urmila do if a supplier keeps sweet-talking her before every deal?
qa.a: She could keep thanking them and always take a night to check the numbers against other quotes.

grounding: The same person separates warmth from steering at two ages: trusting a friend who praises and disagrees over one who flatters for favours, and later thanking a flatterer without letting it decide.

passage: At fifteen, Urmila overheard her aunt at the dinner table: "Save what you can for the wedding fund, Urmila's marriage is what matters. Tushar's fees come first, he is the boy." Urmila stared at her rice. Her brother Tushar looked at her, then down. That night she wondered if she was only a cost to the family, and she did not sleep. The next morning Tushar left a note on her desk. "I think you should keep studying too. I'll say it at dinner." Their father listened, and later said school fees would be paid for both. At twenty-five, Urmila was engaged to Irfan. His uncle said smiling that there was no demand, only custom, and then read out a list: a car, furniture, and a grand hall for five hundred. Urmila's mother went pale. Urmila said quietly, "That is a demand with a friendly name." Irfan put his hand on the list. "It stays off the table. We decide our own wedding." His uncle sighed loudly and said nothing more that evening.

qa.q: Who left the note on Urmila's desk?
qa.a: Her brother Tushar left the note.

qa.q: How does the fund at fifteen connect to the list at twenty-five?
qa.a: At fifteen Urmila was told the wedding fund mattered more than her schooling, and at twenty-five a list of gifts was called custom instead of a demand. In both cases marriage was tied to money and her worth, and equal support from Tushar and Irfan answered it.

qa.q: What was Urmila feeling when she lay awake wondering if she was only a cost to the family?
qa.a: She felt hurt and unwanted, worried that she was a burden.

qa.q: What could Urmila's parents do to make sure both children feel equally valued?
qa.a: They can keep paying for both children's schooling and tell them plainly that the wedding fund does not decide who gets encouragement.

grounding: The same young woman meets pressure tied to marriage at two ages: told to save for a wedding while her brother's schooling comes first, then a list of gifts presented as custom.

passage: When Pankaj was nine, his green parrot flew out of the window. "He'll be back tomorrow," he told his sister Farida, and put out a bowl of seeds by the gate. The next day the bowl was untouched. The next day too. His father Gautam sat beside him and said, "Maybe he will, maybe he won't. Either way I'll help you look." Pankaj cried hard, wrapped in a blanket, then agreed to draw a picture for lost-pet posters. At fifteen, Pankaj had a maths test coming and told everyone, "I'm sure to fail. I'll be lucky to pass." He told his friends the same about science and Hindi. When results arrived, a good mark in maths felt like a gift, and a low one in science hardly stung. But Farida noticed that he had left his textbooks shut, because what would be the point. "You say you'll fail so it won't hurt," she said. "You don't actually think that, do you?" Pankaj shrugged and stared at the ceiling.

qa.q: What did Pankaj put out by the gate for the parrot?
qa.a: He put out a bowl of seeds by the gate.

qa.q: How do Pankaj's expectations at nine and fifteen differ, and what do they share?
qa.a: At nine he was sure the parrot would come back tomorrow, and it hurt when it did not, while at fifteen he expected to fail every exam so any mark felt like a win. Both protect his feelings, but the second also quietly cut his effort.

qa.q: What was Pankaj feeling when he cried hard, wrapped in a blanket, after several days without the parrot?
qa.a: He felt heartbroken and shocked because his hope had been so certain.

qa.q: What could Farida say or do to help Pankaj with his exams?
qa.a: She could ask him what result he really hopes for and offer to study with him, so effort does not stop.

grounding: The same person shows two ways of guarding feelings: a child's fixed rosy view that shatters, and a teenager's defensive pessimism that lowers his effort.

passage: At two, Mahima sat beside another toddler, Parveen, at a nursery table. Parveen banged a spoon, so Mahima banged hers. Parveen pushed away her peas, and Mahima pushed hers, too, though she liked peas at home. They both laughed. At fifteen, Mahima had taken on her group's slang and the way they rolled their sleeves. She agreed to a dare she did not like because everyone said yes. That evening she texted her old friend Parveen, "I feel like I'm doing an impression of myself." Parveen replied, "Come over. You don't have to be anyone." At twenty-five, Mahima worked at a design company where everyone stayed until eight, though the day's work was often done by five. She opened social media and pretended to read reports. Her colleague Kishore stretched and said, "Are we really working, or just sitting?" She laughed, but she could not say whether anyone would notice if she left, and she stayed in her chair, afraid of looking less committed than the rest of them.

qa.q: What did Parveen push away at the nursery table?
qa.a: Parveen pushed away her peas.

qa.q: How does Mahima's copying at two, fifteen and twenty-five change, and what stays the same?
qa.a: At two she copied Parveen's spoon and peas without any idea of rules, at fifteen she took on the group's slang and a dare she disliked to belong, and at twenty-five she stayed late because everyone did, although the work was done. Each time she followed the people around her without asking whether it suited her.

qa.q: What was Mahima feeling when she texted Parveen that she was doing an impression of herself?
qa.a: She felt uneasy and unsure of who she was, tired of pretending to fit in.

qa.q: What could Mahima try at work if she wants to leave when her work is done?
qa.a: She could quietly ask Kishore or a manager whether staying late is really needed, and leave on time once or twice to see what happens.

grounding: The same person conforms across ages: imitation at two, adopting the group's slang and dares at fifteen, and staying late because everyone does at twenty-five.

passage: At the cinema counter, fifteen-year-old Lavanya read the board. Small popcorn: seventy rupees. Large popcorn: two hundred. Medium popcorn with a drink: two hundred and ten. Her brother Shankar grinned. "Get the medium combo, it's basically free!" Lavanya nodded with the smug feeling of a smart shopper, ignoring that she had only wanted a small one and could barely finish half. Five years later, in her hostel, she compared streaming plans on her phone with her roommate Sharmila. The basic plan was cheap, the middle plan cost almost as much as the top plan but had far fewer features, and the top plan had everything. "Premium is obvious," Lavanya said. "The middle one is a joke." Sharmila glanced at the screen and then at the calendar. "You barely watch anything during exams." Lavanya paused, phone in hand. She read the three rows again, slowly, as if they might read differently. Then she wrote her real viewing hours on a scrap of paper beside the plans and compared the numbers.

qa.q: What did Lavanya's brother tell her to get at the cinema?
qa.a: He told her to get the medium combo.

qa.q: How did the third option affect Lavanya's choices at fifteen and twenty?
qa.a: At fifteen a large popcorn at two hundred made the medium combo at two hundred and ten look like a bargain, and at twenty a middle plan almost as costly as premium made premium look obvious. In both cases the poor option in the middle steered her, not her real need.

qa.q: What was Lavanya feeling at the cinema counter after choosing the medium combo?
qa.a: She felt smug and pleased with her smart choice, though it was one she had not needed.

qa.q: What could Lavanya do before picking a plan again?
qa.a: She could write down how much she really uses and wants, then compare each plan against that.

grounding: The same person is steered by a poor third option at two ages: a popcorn combo that looks like a bargain, and a middle streaming plan that makes premium seem obvious.

passage: In Class Four, the teacher held up two ribbons and asked which was longer. Tejas could see plainly that the blue one was. But the first child said red, and so did the second, and the third. By the time it was Tejas's turn, his heart thumped. He looked at the ribbons again. Blue was longer; he was sure. "Red," he said, softly. Ankita, sitting near the window, said, "Blue," and the class giggled. Tejas looked at his shoes and wished he had said it too. At fifteen, Tejas sat with a group who agreed that a new film was brilliant. He had thought it was slow and confused. They also agreed that their classmate Hansa was "so annoying." He had actually found her quick and funny. Everyone nodded. "Yeah," said Tejas. "It was great." On the bus home he found himself wondering if he had misjudged the film and whether perhaps Hansa really was irritating. He could not tell if he had changed his mind or had only kept quiet.

qa.q: Which ribbon did Tejas see was longer?
qa.a: He saw that the blue ribbon was longer.

qa.q: How does Tejas's giving in at the ribbons compare with his giving in at fifteen?
qa.a: At the ribbons he said red although he could see blue was longer, and at fifteen he said the film was great and let Hansa be called annoying although he thought otherwise. The first time he knew he was going along, but the second time he began to doubt his own view.

qa.q: What was Tejas feeling when he said "Red" after the class had picked red?
qa.a: He felt anxious and afraid of being laughed at, so he gave up what he saw.

qa.q: What could Tejas do next time a whole group agrees on something he doubts?
qa.a: He could look for one friend, like Ankita, who sees it differently, or say quietly that he sees it another way.

grounding: The same person conforms under group agreement at two ages: naming the wrong ribbon in a class, and adopting a group's opinion of a film and a classmate at fifteen.
